about.title: Bellflower Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Bellflower packs roughly 78,000 residents into a compact stretch of southeast Los Angeles County, and daily life here runs through busy commercial corridors like Bellflower Boulevard, Alondra Boulevard, Woodruff Avenue and Clark Avenue. Grocery stores, strip-mall parking lots, apartment stairwells and restaurant entryways all come with a basic obligation: the people who control the property are supposed to keep it reasonably safe, or at least warn you when they cannot. When they do not, and you fall, California premises liability law gives you a path to recover for medical bills, lost wages and the disruption to your life. The catch is proof. You generally need to show the owner knew about the hazard, or should have known, and did nothing. That is why what you do in the first days matters so much — photographs, incident reports, witness names and a request that surveillance footage be saved before it is overwritten. LawProactive is not a law firm. We simply connect Bellflower residents with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why Bellflower Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the whole case
items.desc: California requires proof that the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can pursue cleaning logs, maintenance records and prior complaints that show how long the problem sat there.

items.title: Video disappears fast
items.desc: Most Bellflower stores and apartment complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation letter out early can be the difference between a clear picture of the fall and nothing at all.

items.title: Two-year clock, sometimes shorter
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but a fall on city, county or school property triggers a much shorter government-claim window. Connecting with counsel promptly protects both deadlines.

items.question: I slipped in a store parking lot on Bellflower Boulevard and the manager said it was my fault. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California uses pure comparative fault, meaning even if you were partly responsible — say, looking at your phone — you can still recover, with your share reduced by your percentage of fault. The manager's opinion is not a legal ruling. Photograph the spot, get the incident report number and ask in writing that the lot's camera footage be preserved.

items.question: How do I prove the owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Notice can be shown directly, such as a prior complaint or a work order, or indirectly by proving the condition existed long enough that a reasonable inspection would have caught it. Sweep logs, employee schedules, weather records and witness statements all help build that timeline. An attorney can request these records formally, which is difficult to do on your own.

items.question: What if I fell on Bellflower city property, like a sidewalk or a park?
items.answer: Claims against a public entity in California follow a different track with a much shorter deadline — generally you must file a government claim within six months of the injury, well before the standard two-year limit. Missing that window can bar the case entirely. Because the rules differ from a claim against a private business, it is worth speaking with an attorney quickly.
